editor_spans.body: Burnham's Motherwell speech recasts the closure of Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits as failures of geography: decisions 'taken hundreds of miles away' by people who would never live with the consequences. That is a powerful political story. It is also incomplete. Those closures were driven by collapsing demand, global competition and national industrial policy, not only by the distance between Whitehall and Lanarkshire. Moving decision-making closer to Motherwell would not by itself have kept a strip mill open. The risk in Burnham's framing is that devolution gets offered as the cure for deindustrialisation when it is mainly a cure for bad administration.

Set against the scale of that diagnosis, the money on the table is small. The showcase example of the two governments working together is £10 million from each for two defence technical colleges. The research funding is a billion pounds spread across the whole UK. The most substantive offer is a model of localised employment support, while one in six young Scots are not in education, employment or training. That offer extends something Holyrood has partly had since the 2016 Scotland Act devolved some employability programmes. It is a change in who administers support, not in how much there is.

The most concrete lever in the whole speech gets a single anecdote. As mayor, Burnham bought Greater Manchester's buses from Alexander Dennis in Falkirk and accepted a slightly higher price for wider benefits to British communities. Procurement is where a central government can actually steer demand toward places like Lanarkshire, and it needs no new regional bodies. A Prime Minister who means to reindustrialise should be judged on whether Whitehall's purchasing rules change, more than on how many structures are redesigned.

The tone is conciliatory, but the offer carries a competitive edge. Burnham warns that Scottish towns could become 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up', and says Holyrood's own reform programme must 'move faster'. That turns a pitch for partnership into pressure on the SNP government. It is also telling that the National Economic Council will meet the devolved First Ministers for the first time only now. Twenty-seven years into devolution, the machinery for the UK's governments to plan the economy together still barely exists, and that gap is the deeper structural problem the speech circles without naming.
